questions.q: What is the external brain that the author recommends building?
a: A searchable digital store for notes, lists and ideas
A paper journal you review every morning
A personal assistant who manages your calendar
A nightly memory exercise practiced before bed
questions.why: The first lesson suggests a tool like Evernote that holds to-do lists, notes and pictures and lets you search them later.

questions.q: Why does the author say you should stop trying to remember everything?
a: Knowing where to find information is enough
Memory naturally fades faster after age thirty
Recalling facts makes creative thinking harder
Most details are never useful a second time
questions.why: The lesson ends with the idea that knowing means knowing where to find it, so storing everything in a tool is enough.

questions.q: How did Ari make money from his custom wall mount?
a: He sold copies of the design to people with the same computer
He licensed the design to a large furniture retailer
He taught a paid class about 3D printing
He rented the mount out to coworkers each week
questions.why: The second lesson says he sold six more mounts to others who owned the same computer and made 400 dollars.

questions.q: What is an upper limit, as the summary defines it?
a: A maximum amount you decide you cannot exceed
A minimum you promise never to fall below
A deadline for completing a difficult task
A cap on what you are willing to pay for tools
questions.why: Upper limits are maximums, such as a number of clothes or hours on social media; lower limits are minimums.

questions.q: What do upper and lower limits help you do?
a: Trade quantity for quality and protect time for what matters
Fill your working hours more completely each week
Replace the need for to-do lists and calendars
Prove that you can live on less money
questions.why: The third lesson says both limits help you trade quantity for quality so work and possessions do not crowd out what matters.
